newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian envoy reassures Chechen rebels.
newsitem.headline: New Russian envoy reassures Chechen rebels.

text.p: Russia's new security chief met Chechen rebel leaders on Sunday for the first time and said he would stick to the peace deal signed by his ousted predecessor Alexander Lebed.

"The agreement has been signed and every letter of that agreement must be fulfilled. That is my principle policy," Ivan Rybkin said at the meeting with former rebel military commander Aslan Mashkadov and two other separatist leaders.

A source at the meeting said Maskhadov, who swapped his fatigues for a dapper business suit, told Rybkin the rebels objected to Moscow's plans to keep two brigades in Chechnya, saying Lebed agreed that all troops would be withdrawn.
Rybkin told him he was not aware of such a pledge but promised to find out and also argued that the military was having problems finding homes for the troops, the source said.

The separatists have said they are worried that Lebed's dismissal this month could jeopardise the peace deal he signed with them in late August to end 21 months of fighting in the North Caucasus region.
Rybkin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin have been at pains to reassure them that Moscow does not want a return to the violence which killed tens of thousands of people.
But a lasting peace is still a long way off and disagreements continue over control of the breakaway region, which Moscow insists must remain in the Russian Federation.
Earlier rebel leaders attended a congress in southwestern Chechnya at which they said there could be no compromise on independence from Moscow.

Conservative Kremlin officials and members of parliament cite such comments to explain their opposition to the August peace deal, which the rebels treated as a victory in their battle to split Chechnya from Moscow.
The agreement called for the withdrawal of all Russian troops temporarily based in Chechnya and said discussions on the region's future status should be put on hold for five years.

But the rebels later confirmed their plans to seek independence, took Chechnya under their control and unilaterally formed a "coalition government", defying an earlier agreement to cooperate with Russia in creating a post-war authority.

"Chechen independence cannot be subject to trade-offs and compromises," rebel spokesman Ruslan Martagov quoted separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev as telling Sunday's Congress of the Chechen People, Interfax news agency reported.
"After the defeat of the million-strong Russian army, the Chechen people have a right to dictate their conditions to Moscow," Martagov quoted another leader as saying.
About 1,500 delegates approved plans to hold local elections in January and put forward Yandarbiyev as a candidate for president, Itar-Tass news agency said.

The congress opened in a Grozny building but delegates then moved to Urus-Martan, 35 km (20 miles) southwest of the capital, following a telephoned bomb warning, Tass said. An initial police search found no trace of a bomb.
Rybkin met the separatist leaders at an official residence near Nazran, capital of the Ingushetia region neighbouring Chechnya, and later had supper with them.
